title: Focusing: it-clauses and what-clauses
subtitle: It was Olav that ... / What I did was ...
summary: Focus attention on one part of a sentence with an it-clause or a what-clause, and know which wh-words can do the job.

lesson.heading: Focusing with it-clauses
lesson.text: An **it-clause** with *be* focuses attention on whatever comes straight after it. The clause that follows - usually a that-clause - carries information that is already known or less important. Sentences like this are called cleft sentences.

examples.text: 'Lea bought the car from Olav.' 'No, **it was Olav that** bought the car from Lea.'
I don't mind her criticising me, but **it's how she does it that** I object to.
**It was to show** how much I cared for her **that** I bought her the necklace.

lesson.heading: which, who, when, where - but not how or why
lesson.text: We can use **which** or **who** instead of *that*. **when** and **where** are also possible, though usually only in informal English. **how** and **why** cannot replace *that*.

examples.text: Karl was always there to help her, and **it was to him that / who** she now turned for support.
'Ida's seriously ill in hospital.' 'But **it was only last Sunday when / that** I was playing tennis with her.'
**It was in Warsaw where / that** the film was made.
'No, **it was by improving distribution that** he made it profitable.'

lesson.heading: Focusing with what-clauses

left.label: Neutral
examples: We gave them some home-made cake.

right.label: Focus with a what-clause
examples: **What we gave them was** some home-made cake.

lesson.note: The information in focus sits outside the what-clause. This pattern is especially common in conversation.

lesson.heading: What what-clauses are for
lesson.text: We use them to introduce a new topic, to give a reason, instruction or explanation, or to correct something that has been said or done. The what-clause can usually go at either end of the sentence.

examples.text: **What I'd like you to work on is** the revision exercise on the website.
Isa arrived two hours late: **what had happened was that** his bicycle chain had broken.
'We've only got this small bookcase - will that do?' 'No, **what I was looking for was** something much bigger and stronger.'
**What upset me most was** his rudeness. / His rudeness **was what upset me most**.

lesson.heading: Focusing on an action
lesson.text: To focus on an action someone performed, use **what + subject + do + be + to-infinitive**. An it-clause cannot do this.

examples.text: Luis lost his job and was short of money, so **what he did was (to) sell** his flat and move in with his brother.
examples.wrong: it was (to) sell his flat that he did

lesson.heading: Other wh-words: use a noun instead
lesson.text: We don't normally put a *how-, when-, where-, who-* or *why-*clause at the front. Instead we use a noun with a related meaning - **reason** rather than why, **place** rather than where - followed by a that- or wh-clause.

examples.text: **The only reason (why / that)** I left the party early **was that** I was feeling unwell.
examples.note: rather than Why I left the party early was ...

examples.text: **The place (where / that)** you should play football is the playground, not the classroom.
**Somebody (who / that)** I enjoy reading is Peter Carey.
**The time (when / that)** I work best is early morning.

lesson.text: Only *what* can start this kind of focusing clause. For the others, put a noun in front: the reason, the place, the time, somebody.

exercises.prompt: Mark's known for ages that his parents are coming to stay with us this weekend, but it was only yesterday ___ he told me.
exercises.explanation: After a time expression in an it-clause, both that and when are possible.

exercises.statement: It was Olav that bought the car from Lea.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The it-clause puts the focus on Olav; the rest is already known.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Did you say that Rudi was going to live in Austria? *B:* No, ___ was that he was going on holiday to Austria.
exercises.explanation: A what-clause is the natural way to correct what someone has just said.

exercises.prompt: ___ I left the party early was that I was feeling unwell.
exercises.explanation: A why-clause is avoided at the front; use the noun reason instead.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Did it annoy you that Carla came so late? *B:* No, ___ was that she didn't apologise.
exercises.explanation: The what-clause carries the known part; the correction goes at the end.

exercises.statement: It was by improving distribution how he made it profitable.
exercises.explanation: It was by improving distribution that he made it profitable. how cannot replace that in an it-clause.

exercises.prompt: Match the focusing clause with the information it focuses on.

pairs.left: It was to show how much I cared for her
pairs.right: that I bought her the necklace.
that his bicycle chain had broken.

pairs.left: What I'd like you to work on is
pairs.right: the revision exercise on the website.

pairs.left: The place where you should play football is
Somebody who I enjoy reading is

exercises.prompt: *A:* You grew up in this village, didn't you? *B:* In fact the ___ I grew up is between this village and the next.
exercises.explanation: Use the noun place rather than starting the sentence with Where ... .

exercises.prompt: She doesn't find learning languages very easy, and it was only by studying very hard ___ she improved her Spanish.
exercises.explanation: After a by + -ing phrase in an it-clause, only that is possible - not how.

exercises.statement: Why I left the party early was that I was feeling unwell.
exercises.explanation: The only reason (why) I left the party early was that I was feeling unwell. A why-clause is not used in this position.

exercises.prompt: Helena has been feeling a bit depressed for some time, so ... Focus on your reason for booking the holiday.
exercises.answer: it was to cheer her up that I booked a holiday in Amsterdam.
exercises.explanation: The it-clause puts the purpose in focus and leaves the known information for the that-clause.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Did you fly from Sydney to Brisbane? Correct A, focusing on the action.
exercises.answer: No, what I did was hire a car and drive all the way.
alternatives: No, what I did was to hire a car and drive all the way.
exercises.explanation: what + subject + do + be + (to) infinitive focuses on the action performed.
